name: pame meridional, dialecto de Jiliapan / Jiliapan Pame
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Manrique Castañeda 1960.

catalog_locator: FONOLOGÍA, p. 7, last paragraph; p. 13, second paragraph; cf. p. 17, word-melody paragraph.
catalog_quote: Además de estos fonemas segmentales hay tres fonemas de tono-acento: alto (´), bajo (`) y descendente (ˆ), que pueden recaer, solamente uno de ellos, sobre cada palabra. Naturalmente hay tonos secundarios sobre las sílabas no acentuadas de la palabra, y aunque no han sido suficientemente analizados, como para predecir su calidad en cada caso, su producción es mecánica. Considero que el tono-acento es fonémico porque hay pares mínimos diferenciados solamente por él, pero no he encontrado que tenga función gramatical; algunos ejemplos de palabras diferenciadas por el tono, son: kudû diablo / kudù piedra; tikí? flecha / tikî? hule [p. 7] ... las vocales, y sólo ellas, constituyen el núcleo de la sílaba; solamente las vocales llevan el fonema suprasegmental de tono-acento, y cuando no lo llevan tienen tonos secundarios que contrastan con el de la sílaba acentuada (en realidad, en ciertos grupos las nasales m n tienen también tonos secundarios que las convierten en núcleos de sílabas fonéticas, pero no fonémicas). Todas las vocales tienen una cantidad un poco mayor que la de las consonantes, sufren un ligero alargamiento cuando están acentuadas o cuando van en posición final, y un alargamiento mayor cuando reunen las dos condiciones. [p. 13]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: Besides these segmental phonemes there are three tone-accent phonemes: high (´), low (`) and falling (ˆ), of which only one can fall on each word. Naturally there are secondary tones on the unaccented syllables of the word, and although they have not been analyzed enough to predict their quality in each case, their production is mechanical. I consider the tone-accent phonemic because there are minimal pairs differentiated only by it, but I have not found it to have a grammatical function [p. 7] ... only vowels carry the suprasegmental phoneme of tone-accent, and when they do not carry it they have secondary tones that contrast with that of the accented syllable [p. 13]
new_statements.citation: Manrique Castañeda, Leonardo. 1960. Esbozo descriptivo del pame meridional (dialecto de Jiliapan). Tesis de licenciatura en Lingüística, Escuela Nacional de Antropología e Historia, México. 48 pp.
new_statements.locator: FONOLOGÍA, p. 7 (p. 9) and p. 13 (p. 15); cf. p. 17 (p. 19)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (50 pp., image-only scan) and rendered pp. 1, 9, 15 to PNG ( to read the page scan directly, alongside the scanned file we hold. Page 7 (p. 9), section FONOLOGIA, last paragraph, reads exactly as quoted: 'Además de estos fonemas segmentales hay tres fonemas de tono-acento: alto (´), bajo (`) y descendente (ˆ), que pueden recaer, solamente uno de ellos, sobre cada palabra. Naturalmente hay tonos secundarios sobre las sílabas no acentuadas de la palabra, y aunque no han sido suficientemente analizados, como para predecir su calidad en cada caso, su producción es mecánica. Considero que el tono-acento es fonémico porque hay pares mínimos diferenciados solamente por él, pero no he encont…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Each word has exactly one prominent ('tone-accented') syllable, which carries one of three contrastive tones (high, low, falling); all other syllables bear non-contrastive, mechanically produced secondary tones, and accented vowels are slightly lengthened. The position of the tone-accent within the word is NOT stated anywhere in the thesis (nor in the 1967 English snippets); examples show it on different syllables (kudû/kudù 'devil/stone', tikí? 'arrow', mpúhar 'horse'). Berthiaume (2012: 9) infers root stress from Manrique 1967, but that is his inference. Manrique's 'tono-acento' is a fused tone-stress unit, so a pitch accent reading is also defensible.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None as stress; 'tonos secundarios' (secondary tones) on unaccented syllables, described as mechanical/predictable but not analyzed (p. 7, p. 13).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. In certain clusters the nasals m, n also carry secondary tones and become phonetic (not phonemic) syllable peaks (p. 13). Tone-accent has no grammatical function, unlike other Pamean languages.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('sobre cada palabra'); p. 17 adds that each word thereby has its own melody and that phrase melody rises slowly and falls abruptly at the end, with no declarative/interrogative difference. Data from two Jiliapan informants (Abundia Santana Bartolejo, María Andablo), 1958 and 1960, when only 4-5 speakers remained.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the Jiliapan (Hidalgo) dialect of Southern Pame, which Manrique treats as one of three closely related Southern Pame dialects (Jiliapan, Pacula, Tilaco -- the last already lost by 1960); Jiliapan Pame = sout2999 (no separate glottocode). Schuller 1925 (Valle) is 18th-c. Sierra Gorda Pame (Jalpan/Landa/Tilaco), also within sout2999 territory but a different, earlier variety.

tone_statements.citation: Bartholomew, Doris. 1965. The reconstruction of Otopamean (Mexico). PhD dissertation, University of Chicago.
tone_statements.quote: North Pame, as described by Gibson, has a tone-stress system where stress normally falls on the root syllable and there is a contrast of high, low, and falling pitches. Contrastively, stress may occur on the prefix syllable, and in that case the pitch is always high. The pitches on non-stressed syllables are predictable. Leonardo Manrique postulates a similar tone system for South Pame.

tone_statements.summary: Second-hand, one sentence: SP is said to have a tone system 'similar' to NP's tone-stress system (stress on the root syllable, H/L/F contrast on the stressed syllable, contrastive prefix stress always high, unstressed pitches predictable). That matches the catalog's tonal / pitch accent coding with one stress per word, but the SP details are not spelled out; SP is absent from Table 10. Bartholomew

tone_statements.citation: Soustelle, Jacques. 1937. La famille Otomi-Pame du Mexique central. Travaux et mémoires de l'Institut d'Ethnologie 26. Paris: Institut d'Ethnologie. (Spanish ed. 1993, La familia otomí-pame del México central, FCE.)
tone_statements.quote: 3. Accent. L'accent tombe en general sur la derniere syllabe des mots ; dans ce cas, comme nous l'avons fait pour l'otomi, nous ne le marquons pas. Mais, lorsqu'un mot prend un suffixe tel que -t (pluriel), -n (feminin), etc... il garde l'accent sur sa derniere syllabe, c'est-a-dire sur la penultieme de l'expression formee par suffixation. Ainsi pahal (cheval) devra etre lu pahal, et au pluriel nous ecrivons, en marquant l'accent, yuhalot. Il nous a fallu avoir recours a une convention speciale pour les groupes des deux voyelles si frequents en pame a la fin des mots. Dans la majorite des cas, l'accent se place sur la premiere voyelle. [...] dans les rares cas ou il tombe sur la deuxieme voyelle, nous le marquerons. [...] nous ecrirons limpias (tissu d'ixtle), nannod (aile), avec un accent. || Tone: 'En ce qui concerne le pame, je puis preciser que les tons n'y jouent aucun role.'

tone_statements.summary: Catalog codes sout2999 as tonal (tone_cls pitch accent, after Manrique 1960). Soustelle 1937 states outright that tones play no role in Pame and describes a single word accent, generally on the last syllable of the word; suffixed forms (-t plural, -n feminine) keep the stem-final accent, so it becomes penultimate; word-final two-vowel groups take the accent on the first vowel in most cases, rarely

sources.note: FONOLOGÍA p. 7: three 'tono-acento' phonemes (alto, bajo, descendente), only one per word; secondary tones on unstressed syllables are mechanical; tone-accent is phonemic (minimal pairs kudû 'diablo' / kudù 'piedra') with no grammatical function. p. 13: only vowels carry the tone-accent; unstressed syllables bear secondary tones contrasting with the accented syllable; vowels lengthen slightly when accented or word-final. p. 17: each word has its own melody. No rule for the position of the tone-accent is given. Scan verified against the page scan (pp. 7, 13, 17).
